text:
[
  {
    "n": 1,
    "title": "Fundamental Roles and Abstractions of the Operating System",
    "scope": "Defines what an operating system is from top-down and bottom-up perspectives. Explains how the OS acts as an extended machine providing clean hardware abstractions such as files and sockets to developers. Details the OS role as a resource manager that governs resource allocation via time multiplexing and space multiplexing.",
    "key_points": [
      "Definition of an operating system as an intermediary software layer between application software and raw hardware",
      "Top-down perspective: the OS as an extended machine that hides device-level hardware quirks behind uniform abstractions (e.g., files for disk blocks)",
      "Bottom-up perspective: the OS as a resource manager providing controlled, orderly allocation of CPUs, memories, and I/O devices",
      "Time multiplexing: sharing a resource sequentially by taking turns (e.g., CPU scheduling, printer queues)",
      "Space multiplexing: partitioning a physical resource simultaneously among multiple consumers (e.g., main memory regions, disk block allocations)"
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 2,
    "title": "CPU Execution Modes, Hardware Protection, and Traps",
    "scope": "Teaches the architectural division between kernel mode and user mode, detailing why dual-mode execution is essential for system stability. Explains the mechanisms of privileged instructions, I/O restrictions, and the TRAP mechanism for system calls. Covers the protection boundaries that isolate software crashes, contrasting user-mode recovery with catastrophic kernel panics.",
    "key_points": [
      "Kernel mode (supervisor mode): execution with complete, unrestricted access to hardware, all memory addresses, and privileged CPU instructions",
      "User mode: restricted execution context where hardware control instructions, direct memory addressing outside the process space, and direct I/O are forbidden",
      "System call mechanism: issuing a software interrupt (TRAP) to cross privilege boundaries from user mode into the kernel",
      "Protection and fault isolation: user-mode application crashes kill only the offending process and remain fully recoverable, whereas faults in kernel mode halt the operating system"
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 3,
    "title": "Historical Generations of Operating Systems",
    "scope": "Surveys the evolution of operating systems across five technological generations from 1945 to the present. Explains how shifts in underlying physical hardware forced corresponding innovations in software architecture, from plugboards to mobile operating systems. Clarifies the theoretical differences between batch multiprogramming, spooling, and interactive time-sharing.",
    "key_points": [
      "1st Generation (1945–1955): vacuum tubes and plugboards (ENIAC, Colossus); absence of an operating system, direct mechanical and machine-language rewiring",
      "2nd Generation (1955–1965): transistors, core memory, magnetic tapes/disks; introduction of batch systems to sequence mainframe jobs automatically",
      "3rd Generation Part 1 (1965–1971): integrated circuits (SSI/MSI), high-level languages, and the introduction of multiprogramming, spooling, and time-sharing (e.g., IBM System/360, PDP)",
      "Conceptual contrast: multiprogramming runs multiple jobs concurrently on one system to maximize CPU utilization; time-sharing multiplexes CPU time slices among interactive users (all time-sharing systems are multiprogramming systems, but not all multiprogramming systems are time-sharing)",
      "3rd Generation Part 2 (1971–1980): microprocessors (LSI/VLSI), RAID storage, data communications, and early parallel/AI applications",
      "4th Generation (1980–1990): personal computing enabled by LSI; Intel 8080 CPU, 8-inch floppy disks, CP/M, and the IBM PC",
      "5th Generation (1990–present): mobile, ubiquitous computing, handheld devices, and pervasive network connectivity"
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 4,
    "title": "Processor Architecture, Instruction Execution, and Pipelines",
    "scope": "Reviews core CPU mechanics essential for operating system design. Covers the six phases of the instruction machine cycle and the architectural roles of dedicated internal registers. Explains how pipelining and superscalar execution accelerate instruction throughput at the hardware level.",
    "key_points": [
      "Six-step CPU instruction cycle: Fetch Instruction, Decode Instruction, Calculate Operands, Fetch Operands, Execute Instruction, and Write Operand",
      "General-purpose registers: internal high-speed storage for intermediate variables and computational results",
      "Program Counter (PC): holds the memory address of the next instruction to be fetched",
      "Stack Pointer (SP): points to the current top of the call and activation stack in memory",
      "Program Status Word (PSW): status register holding condition flags (comparison outcomes), CPU priority level, and current execution mode (kernel vs. user)",
      "Three-stage instruction pipeline: concurrent execution overlapping Fetch, Decode, and Execute stages across sequential instructions",
      "Superscalar CPU architecture: duplicate parallel execution units fed by an instruction holding buffer to retire more than one instruction per clock cycle"
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 5,
    "title": "Processor Concurrency: Multithreading, Hyper-Threading, and Multicore",
    "scope": "Teaches the structural differences between hardware multithreading, hyper-threading, and multicore parallelism. Details how the OS schedules threads and processes across physical cores and logical processors. Analyzes workload execution times and CPU-bound scheduling bottlenecks on hyperthreaded multicore systems.",
    "key_points": [
      "Hardware multithreading / Hyper-Threading: duplicating architectural thread states (registers) on a single physical core to allow zero-cycle or nanosecond context switching when a thread stalls on memory",
      "True parallelism vs. hardware concurrency: hyper-threading multiplexes execution units on one physical core without true instruction parallelism; multicore chips integrate distinct physical CPUs on a die for true simultaneous execution",
      "Cache topologies in multicore chips: independent per-core L1 caches paired with either shared L2 caches or dedicated per-core L2 caches",
      "Graphics Processing Units (GPUs): massively parallel architectures comprising thousands of small, specialized cores optimized for uniform data-parallel tasks",
      "Scheduling and execution analysis on dual-core hyperthreaded topologies: calculating program completion times for CPU-bound tasks based on physical CPU vs. logical processor thread co-location"
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 6,
    "title": "The Memory Hierarchy and Caching Performance",
    "scope": "Presents the memory hierarchy model, detailing trade-offs among access speed, capacity, and cost per bit. Covers the internal organization of caches, cache lines, and fundamental cache management challenges. Formulates and solves the mathematical model for Average Memory Access Time (AMAT) across multi-level memory systems.",
    "key_points": [
      "Four-tier memory pyramid: Registers (<1 KB, ~1 ns), Cache (~4 MB, ~2 ns), Main Memory (1–8 GB, ~10 ns), and Magnetic Disk (1–4 TB, ~10 ms / 10,000,000 ns)",
      "Cache line granularity: memory transfers between RAM and cache organized in fixed chunks (typically 64 bytes)",
      "Cache hit mechanics: CPU fetches from cache on hit without bus transactions (~2 clock cycles); cache misses force main memory access",
      "Four core caching design decisions: when to fetch new lines, placement policy, replacement/eviction policy, and write-back/write-through destination",
      "Average Memory Access Time (AMAT) derivation: AMAT = h_c * t_c + (1 - h_c) * h_m * t_m + (1 - h_c) * (1 - h_m) * t_d, where h is hit rate and t is access latency"
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 7,
    "title": "Storage Media, Disk Geometry, and Hardware Sizing",
    "scope": "Explains the characteristics and roles of primary non-volatile memory technologies including ROM, EEPROM, Flash, and CMOS. Details the mechanical structure and operational geometry of multi-platter hard disk drives. Derives the formulas for disk I/O latency components and memory footprint calculations for display framebuffers.",
    "key_points": [
      "Memory technologies: volatile RAM, factory-programmed ROM, rewritable EEPROM, block-erasable Flash memory (subject to write wear-out), and low-power battery-backed CMOS for system clock and boot configurations",
      "Multi-platter hard disk physical anatomy: rotating platters, read/write heads, actuator arm, concentric tracks, sectors, and arc segments",
      "Disk I/O latency equation: Total Access Time = Seek Time (mechanical head arm positioning) + Rotational Delay/Latency (platter spin to sector) + Transfer Time (data rate over track)",
      "Display memory calculation: monochrome character buffer (e.g., 25 lines * 80 columns = 2,000 bytes) versus uncompressed 24-bit RGB bitmap framebuffers (e.g., 1200 * 900 * 3 bytes = 3,240,000 bytes)"
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 8,
    "title": "I/O Architecture, Device Drivers, and Data Transfer Mechanisms",
    "scope": "Covers the interaction between the operating system, device controllers, and physical peripherals. Contrasts memory-mapped I/O with port-mapped I/O using dedicated machine instructions. Compares the three foundational I/O transfer mechanisms: polling/busy waiting, interrupt-driven I/O, and Direct Memory Access (DMA).",
    "key_points": [
      "I/O device partition: low-level hardware device paired with an electronic device controller exposing control, status, and data registers",
      "Device drivers: kernel-mode software modules that encapsulate controller-specific command protocols into standard OS abstractions",
      "Register addressing paradigms: Memory-Mapped I/O (controller registers mapped into OS address space) versus I/O Port Space (separate bus space manipulated via IN and OUT assembly instructions)",
      "Programmed I/O (Busy Waiting / Polling): driver loops continuously reading status registers until hardware completes, tying up the CPU",
      "Interrupt-Driven I/O: controller asserts interrupt line upon completion; CPU indexes into the interrupt vector table to dispatch the corresponding interrupt service routine (ISR)",
      "Direct Memory Access (DMA): dedicated hardware controller configured by the CPU to transfer data blocks directly between device registers and main memory, interrupting the CPU only upon total completion"
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 9,
    "title": "System Interconnects, Bus Topologies, and Plug-and-Play",
    "scope": "Examines bus architectures connecting system components, contrasting shared bus arbitration with point-to-point serial topologies. Surveys modern bus standards and their specialized system roles. Explains the operational principles of Plug-and-Play (PnP) resource allocation.",
    "key_points": [
      "Shared bus architecture: multiple devices arbitrated across common physical wires, requiring bus arbiters to resolve bus contention",
      "Parallel vs. serial bus structures: parallel buses transmit complete words across wide physical lanes (e.g., legacy PCI); serial architectures transmit packetized bitstreams over high-speed differential pairs (e.g., PCIe lanes)",
      "System bus hierarchy: DDR3/DDR4 (high-bandwidth memory bus), PCIe (graphics and fast peripherals), DMI (chipset interconnect link between northbridge and southbridge), SATA/SCSI (storage attachments), and USB (centralized host-polled serial bus)",
      "Plug-and-Play (PnP) mechanism: replacing static jumper-configured hardware with automated boot-time device discovery, dynamically assigning non-conflicting Interrupt Request (IRQ) levels and I/O register address ranges"
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 10,
    "title": "The Computer Bootstrapping Sequence",
    "scope": "Details the deterministic step-by-step procedure required to bootstrap a computer from power-on to user interface availability. Covers motherboard firmware execution, memory diagnostics, device scanning, and multi-stage boot loader execution. Explains how the OS initializes kernel tables, drivers, and background daemons.",
    "key_points": [
      "Power-On Self-Test (POST): firmware routine executing from ROM/BIOS to verify motherboard integrity, detect installed RAM, and validate core peripherals",
      "Bus scanning and boot device selection: firmware queries attached buses and selects a boot medium according to configuration priorities stored in CMOS memory",
      "Master Boot Record (MBR) and active partition table: first sector of the boot medium loaded at fixed memory addresses; examines partition table to identify the bootable partition",
      "Secondary boot loader: loads the kernel binary image from the active partition into main memory and transfers execution control",
      "Operating system initialization: OS queries BIOS for hardware configuration tables, loads matching device drivers into kernel space, initializes internal process and memory tables, spawns system daemons, and launches the login shell or GUI"
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 11,
    "title": "The Operating System Zoo: Specialized OS Classes",
    "scope": "Provides a comprehensive taxonomy of modern operating systems, classifying them by physical scale, resource constraints, and operational goals. Explores the unique operational requirements of mainframes, servers, embedded systems, sensor nodes, real-time environments, and smart cards.",
    "key_points": [
      "Mainframe operating systems (e.g., OS/390): optimized for massive concurrent I/O throughput across batch processing, high-volume transaction processing, and multi-tenant database timesharing",
      "Server operating systems (e.g., Linux, FreeBSD, Windows Server, Solaris): network-centric multi-user platforms providing file, web, and database services while sharing hardware resources",
      "Multiprocessor and Personal Computer operating systems: desktop platforms supporting symmetric multiprocessing, graphical user interfaces, and responsive interactive workloads",
      "Handheld and mobile operating systems (e.g., Android, iOS): optimized for touch interaction, energy preservation, and integrated wireless communication",
      "Embedded operating systems (e.g., VxWorks, Embedded Linux): run dedicated appliances (microwaves, cars, avionics) with fixed hardware and locked software execution environments",
      "Sensor-node operating systems (e.g., TinyOS): extremely lightweight event-driven kernels running on resource-starved microcontrollers equipped with wireless radios",
      "Real-Time Operating Systems (RTOS, e.g., QNX): systems governed by strict temporal predictability, distinguished into hard real-time (absolute deterministic deadlines where misses cause catastrophe) and soft real-time (occasional deadline misses cause quality degradation but not failure)",
      "Smart card operating systems: ultra-minimalist kernels residing on credit-card secure chips, frequently running a constrained Java Virtual Machine (Java Card) to interpret bytecoded applets"
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 12,
    "title": "UNIX System Architecture, Standard Streams, and Shell Process Control",
    "scope": "Establishes the layered architectural model of UNIX systems separating hardware, kernel, shell, and user processes. Teaches the shell's role as a text command interpreter, command-line syntax parsing, and standard I/O communication channels. Covers process lifecycle and job control mechanics across foreground, background, and stopped states.",
    "key_points": [
      "Layered UNIX architectural rings: concentric hierarchy with Hardware at the core, followed by the Kernel, the Shell (TUI interpreter), and outermost User Programs",
      "Command structure parsing: decomposing command lines into executable command names, modifying flags/options, and target arguments",
      "Standard communication streams: standard input (stdin, channel 0), standard output (stdout, channel 1), and standard error (stderr, channel 2)",
      "I/O redirection and pipelines: redirecting streams to/from files using <, >, and chaining the stdout of one program to the stdin of another via pipelines (|)",
      "Process execution states and job control: blocking foreground processes vs. non-blocking background processes executed with the ampersand (&)",
      "Process state transitions: suspending foreground jobs via Ctrl+Z (transition to Stopped), killing processes via Ctrl+C, inspecting active jobs with 'jobs', and moving execution between background and foreground using 'bg' and 'fg'"
    ]
  }
]
